nameStory: Chain speedwell gets its name from the way its flowers are arranged in loose chains or clusters along the stem, creating a linked appearance. The 'speedwell' part comes from an old English farewell blessing meaning 'may you prosper' - these hardy little plants were thought to bring good luck to travelers.
description: Chain speedwell is a low-growing perennial wildflower that loves wet places. This delicate plant spreads along the ground or floats partially in water, with small oval leaves and tiny pink or white flowers clustered along its stems. It rarely grows taller than a foot, instead preferring to creep and sprawl through marshy areas and pond edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink or white flowers with four rounded petals arranged in loose clusters along the stems - each flower is only about 1/4 inch across and has a delicate, papery texture

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, with a smooth, slightly succulent feel and no teeth along the edges

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Creeps along wet ground or floats partially submerged in shallow water, with stems that feel soft and somewhat spongy when squeezed

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found in or very close to water - if the ground doesn't squelch under your feet, you're probably not looking at chain speedwell

habitat: Look for chain speedwell in marshes, along pond and lake edges, in slow-moving streams, and in wet ditches throughout New England. It thrives in muddy or sandy soils that stay consistently moist or flooded. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other water-loving plants.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early, with fresh green leaves appearing as soon as the ice melts. Plants begin to spread and establish in their watery homes.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time with small pink or white blooms appearing in loose clusters. This is the best time to spot and identify the plant.
seasonality.fall: Flowering may continue into early fall in favorable conditions. Seeds develop and disperse, often floating to new locations.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to the roots in frozen areas, leaving little trace above ground until spring returns.

funFact: Chain speedwell is like nature's own floating garden - it can actually survive completely submerged underwater for short periods, with special air-filled spaces in its stems that work like tiny life preservers to keep it afloat!
confusionNotes: Chain speedwell is most easily confused with other water-loving speedwells like American brooklime or blue water-speedwell, but chain speedwell's pink flowers (rather than blue) and its preference for floating or creeping rather than standing upright help distinguish it.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'pink water speedwell' in some references, the flowers can actually be white as well as pink. This plant is part of a huge speedwell family with nearly 20 species in New England, making it one of our most diverse wildflower groups.
compareHints: Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit. While American brooklime also loves water, it tends to grow more upright with blue flowers, and marsh speedwell has narrower leaves and different flower arrangements.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
